title: HE CAME WITH A SPEAR. HE LEFT WITHOUT IT. THE BIBLE NEVER EVEN TELLS US HIS NAME.
paragraphs: HE CAME WITH A SPEAR. HE LEFT WITHOUT IT. THE BIBLE NEVER EVEN TELLS US HIS NAME.

An Egyptian warrior walked into a fight carrying the weapon that should have guaranteed his victory. But Benaiah took that very spear and turned it against him. Hidden inside this brief, brutal account in 2 Samuel 23:21 is a confrontation with fear, false confidence, and the deeper question every human soul must eventually answer: What are you trusting to save you?
He had a spear.
The other man had a staff.
And somehow, the man holding the spear was the one who died.
Read that again.
Because sometimes the most terrifying thing about a battle is not the weapon your enemy carries.
It is discovering that the thing you trusted to protect you cannot save you.

Somewhere in the history of ancient Israel, a formidable Egyptian warrior faced a man named Benaiah. Scripture does not tell us why they fought, what words they exchanged, or what thoughts crossed their minds.
But it tells us something extraordinary about the outcome.
The Egyptian's own spear became the instrument of his defeat.
And the Bible gives us this detail without even recording his name.
Think about that.
A man remembered for his strength. Remembered for his weapon. Remembered for his death.
But not remembered by name.
There is something deeply unsettling about that.
We spend so much of our lives trying to become unforgettable. We build reputations. We defend our image. We accumulate achievements, possessions, influence, and approval.
We convince ourselves that if we can become strong enough, successful enough, respected enough, nobody will ever be able to bring us down.
Then Scripture introduces a warrior whose impressive weapon could not secure his future.
And suddenly, an ancient battlefield begins asking questions about the modern human heart.
What happens when the thing you have trusted most is not strong enough to save you?
The account appears among the exploits of David's mighty men.
In 2 Samuel 23:21, the King James Version records:
"He slew an Egyptian, a goodly man: and the Egyptian had a spear in his hand; but he went down to him with a staff, and plucked the spear out of the Egyptian's hand, and slew him with his own spear."
That is the entire confrontation as Samuel records it.
No lengthy dialogue.
No elaborate description of the battlefield.
No dramatic speech before the fighting began.
An Egyptian warrior. A spear. Benaiah. A staff.
Then the reversal.
But there is more here than a dramatic ending.
And to understand it faithfully, we need to look closely at what Scripture actually says.
The warrior who killed the Egyptian was Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada, one of David's distinguished fighting men.
His name appears in the Hebrew as בְּנָיָהוּ (Benayahu), commonly understood to mean "Yahweh has built" or "Yahweh has established."
It is a striking name.
But we must be careful not to turn the meaning of a name into a promise the passage never makes.
The biblical author is honoring Benaiah's courage and military accomplishments. He is not telling every believer that God will make them physically invincible.
The surrounding verses help us see why Benaiah was remembered.
In 2 Samuel 23:20, he is described as a valiant man who performed mighty deeds. He struck down two formidable warriors of Moab, and he also killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day.
Then comes the Egyptian.
And the parallel account in 1 Chronicles 11:23 gives us another remarkable detail.
The Egyptian was five cubits tall.
Using a common cubit estimate, that would be approximately seven and a half feet, or 2.3 meters, although the precise measurement depends on the cubit used.
Chronicles also describes the Egyptian's spear as resembling a weaver's beam.
This was no ordinary opponent.
The text presents him as exceptionally imposing, physically formidable, and heavily armed.
But notice something important.
The Bible does not identify this Egyptian warrior by name.
We do not know his personal history, his family, his motives, or whether he ever heard about Israel's God.
We should not invent those details.
And we should not claim that Scripture identifies him as a demon, a giant from the Nephilim, or a supernatural being.
It does not.
What we know is enough.
He was a formidable Egyptian warrior who carried a spear, and Benaiah defeated him using that very weapon.
The Hebrew text makes the reversal especially vivid.
The expression וַיִּגְזֹל אֶת־הַחֲנִית (vayyigzol et-haḥanit) means, in context, "and he seized the spear."
The verb carries the sense of taking or snatching away.
The weapon that belonged to the Egyptian was forcibly taken from him.
And the concluding words describe Benaiah killing him בַּחֲנִיתוֹ (baḥanito) — "with his spear."
His own spear.
The narrative deliberately draws our attention to that reversal.
The man who began the encounter holding the more formidable weapon did not finish it holding that weapon.
Now imagine the scene without pretending to know details Scripture has not given us.
A warrior stands armed with a spear.
Another approaches with a staff.
At some point, the spear changes hands.
And the outcome changes with it.
What seemed to be the Egyptian's advantage becomes the means of his defeat.
There is something about that reversal that reaches beyond the battlefield.
Not because every enemy we face will be defeated in the same way.
Not because every hardship is a divine trap set for somebody else.
And certainly not because followers of Jesus are commanded to seek violence or revenge.
But because Scripture repeatedly exposes the limits of human strength.
The things we consider unshakable can fail.
The things we believe make us untouchable can disappear.
And the confidence we place in ourselves can prove terribly fragile.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
Maybe your spear was money.
You thought that if you earned enough, saved enough, and secured enough, you would finally feel safe.
But the anxiety remained.
Maybe your spear was your reputation.
You worked tirelessly to make people admire you. You hid your struggles, covered your mistakes, and learned how to smile even when your heart was falling apart.
You became so good at appearing strong that nobody knew you needed help.
Maybe your spear was control.
You planned everything. Managed everyone. Anticipated every possible disaster.
And when life refused to follow your plan, you discovered how frightened you were underneath all that confidence.
Or perhaps your spear was something you never wanted anyone to know about.
A secret relationship.
An addiction.
A bitterness you had been feeding for years.
A private compromise you kept defending.
You told yourself you could stop whenever you wanted.
You told yourself nobody would find out.
You told yourself you were still in control.
Until one day, the thing you thought you controlled began controlling you.
And now you understand why this ancient story feels uncomfortably close.
But we need to make a distinction.

The Egyptian's spear was a literal weapon in a historical battle. Our struggles with pride, sin, fear, and misplaced trust are applications we draw from the account, not hidden meanings the text explicitly assigns to his weapon.
The passage itself celebrates Benaiah's courage.
The wider testimony of Scripture invites us to examine where our confidence truly belongs.
And that is where the story becomes more than an account of an extraordinary warrior.
Because the Bible does not merely ask whether you are strong.
It asks whether your strength is anchored in the right place.
Psalm 20:7 declares:
"Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God."
In the ancient world, chariots and horses represented military strength, resources, and power.
They were not imaginary advantages.
They were real.
But they were never ultimate.
And that distinction matters.
You can have intelligence and still need wisdom.
You can have wealth and still lack peace.
You can have influence and still be spiritually lost.
You can have religious knowledge and still refuse to surrender to God.
You can even appear victorious in public while privately losing a battle nobody else can see.
The frightening thing about misplaced confidence is that it often feels like security until the moment it fails.
And sometimes the hardest confession a person can make is not "I am weak."
It is this:
"I have been trusting something more than I have been trusting God."
Perhaps that confession has been sitting inside you for a long time.
You have prayed, but only after exhausting every other option.
You have read Scripture, but avoided the passages that confronted your behavior.
You have asked God to bless your plans without genuinely asking whether your plans honor Him.
You have wanted His protection without surrendering your pride.
His forgiveness without repentance.
His comfort without His correction.
And somewhere along the way, Christianity became something you carried instead of a life transformed by the One you claimed to follow.
That realization can hurt.
But conviction is not the same as condemnation.
The gospel does not reveal our sin merely to leave us drowning in shame.
It reveals our need so that we may turn toward the Savior.
And here we must look beyond Benaiah.
Because as remarkable as his victory was, Benaiah was not the Messiah.
He was a warrior serving during David's reign.
His military achievements did not purchase forgiveness for humanity.
His courage did not reconcile sinners to God.
His victory over the Egyptian did not defeat death itself.
Only Jesus Christ accomplishes the salvation that no human warrior could ever secure.
And this is where the story of the spear leads us toward a far greater question.
What happens when humanity faces an enemy that no amount of courage, wealth, status, or human achievement can overcome?
What happens when the enemy is sin?
What happens when the consequence is death?
What happens when the strongest person you know is still powerless to make himself righteous before a holy God?
Romans 3:23 answers without flattery:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God."
All.
The respected and the rejected.
The wealthy and the poor.
The religious and the rebellious.
The person who sins openly and the person who hides it behind a polished appearance.
No amount of outward strength can erase inward guilt.
No reputation can purchase redemption.
No human accomplishment can cancel the debt of sin.
But the story does not end with our helplessness.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
Read those words slowly.
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we had earned another opportunity.
Not after we had successfully hidden every shameful chapter.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
This is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin does not matter.
It matters so deeply that the Son of God gave Himself to redeem sinners.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
Jesus calls people to repent and believe the gospel.
But that mercy reaches people who could never save themselves.
And now consider the cross.
Jesus was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
His enemies believed they had silenced Him.
The cross was an instrument of Roman execution, designed to humiliate and destroy.
Yet through His willing sacrifice, Christ accomplished the redemption that sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Colossians 2:14–15 speaks of God canceling the record of debt against us through Christ and triumphing over hostile powers through Him.
Hebrews 2:14 explains that through death Jesus would destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil.
And 1 Corinthians 15:54–57 celebrates the victory over death that God gives through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Do you see the greater reversal?
The cross, an instrument of shame and death, became the place where the sinless Savior offered Himself for the guilty.
And the resurrection declared that death would not have the final word.
There is a meaningful thematic connection here with the reversal in Benaiah's battle.
But we should not claim that 2 Samuel 23:21 directly prophesies the crucifixion or that the Egyptian's spear represents Satan.
Scripture does not say that.
Benaiah's victory is a historical act of military courage.
Christ's victory is the unique, saving work of the Son of God.
The comparison is an illustration, not an equation.
And the difference makes the gospel even more extraordinary.
Benaiah defeated an enemy by taking his weapon.
Jesus conquered through giving His own life.
Benaiah survived his encounter.
Jesus willingly entered death and rose again.
Benaiah's victory earned him honor among David's mighty men.
Jesus' victory opens the way for sinners to receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
One was a remarkable warrior.
The other is the risen Lord.
And there is no comparison between their ultimate significance.
Yet there is one more detail worth noticing in the story of Benaiah.
His exploits are recorded among the mighty men associated with King David.
He served a king.
And his story is preserved within the history of that kingdom.
Jesus Christ is the promised Son of David, whose kingdom is everlasting.
But unlike earthly kings, He is not dependent on the strength of soldiers to establish His saving reign.
He is the King who gave Himself for His people.
And He calls us not merely to admire His power, but to follow Him.
That means something for the person reading this with a burdened conscience.
Because maybe your greatest struggle today is not an enemy standing in front of you.
Maybe it is the person you have become while trying to survive.
You have learned to defend yourself before anyone even accuses you.
You have learned to strike with words because you are afraid of being wounded.
You have learned to hide behind anger because admitting grief feels unbearable.
You have learned to appear spiritually strong because you are terrified that people might discover how exhausted your faith has become.
And perhaps you have carried that burden so long that you no longer remember what it feels like to be honest before God.
You worship.
You smile.
You encourage others.
You post verses.
But late at night, when there is nobody left to impress, you know something is wrong.
You are tired of pretending.
Tired of fighting the same temptation.
Tired of asking forgiveness and returning to the same compromise.
Tired of measuring your worth by whether other people approve of you.
Tired of carrying a version of yourself that looks stronger than you feel.
Listen carefully.
You do not need to manufacture a flawless testimony before coming to Christ.
You need to come to Him truthfully.
You do not need to disguise your sin as a harmless mistake.
You need to confess it and turn away from it.
You do not need to pretend your wounds are healed.
You can bring your suffering to the One who is merciful and faithful.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
That is not permission to keep sinning without repentance.
It is an invitation to stop hiding.
Grace does not tell us that our rebellion was harmless.
Grace tells us that forgiveness is possible because Jesus Christ paid a price we could never pay.
And genuine faith does not leave us comfortably enslaved to the same old life.
It calls us into transformation.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated "repentance," refers to a change of mind or turning, with biblical repentance involving a genuine turning toward God and away from sin.
It is more than feeling bad because you were caught.
More than crying because you suffered consequences.
More than promising to change while secretly planning to return.
It is the surrender of a heart that has finally recognized the truth.
"I cannot save myself."
"I cannot keep defending what God calls sin."
"I need Jesus."
And perhaps those are the words you have been afraid to say.
Because surrender feels frightening when you have spent your entire life believing that strength means never letting go.
But Jesus does not call you to save yourself through your own strength.
He calls you to trust Him.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of works, so that no one may boast.
Even your most impressive accomplishments cannot become your Savior.
Even your deepest failures do not place you beyond the reach of Christ's mercy if you turn to Him.
That is why the gospel is not simply a message for people whose lives look respectable.
It is good news for the ashamed.
For the repentant.
For the exhausted.
For the person who knows what it means to fall and desperately wants to walk in the light again.
For the person whose past has become a prison.
For the person who has been called a failure so many times that the word has begun to sound like a name.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
It does not have authority to overrule what Jesus Christ can do in a surrendered life.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
This does not mean every earthly consequence disappears the moment someone believes.
It does not mean trauma vanishes instantly, broken relationships automatically repair themselves, or every struggle ends overnight.
Christian transformation often involves a lifelong process of repentance, growth, obedience, healing, and dependence upon the Holy Spirit.
But it does mean that belonging to Christ changes the deepest foundation of a person's identity and future.
The past is no longer the final authority.
Sin is no longer the rightful master.
Death is no longer the final destination for those who belong to Him.
And that is why our message at Gospel Warrior is more than a memorable phrase.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because He calls evil good.
Not because He removes the need for truth, accountability, repentance, or restitution.
But because He can redeem people who could never redeem themselves.
He can bring light into a life once ruled by darkness.
He can teach the proud to become humble.
He can teach the bitter to forgive.
He can restore the fallen to faithful obedience.
He can give hope to someone who believed their story had already ended.
And maybe that someone is you.
Before you move on, I want to ask you something personal.
What is the spear you have been holding?
What have you been trusting to keep you safe, worthy, important, or in control?
Is it your money?
Your reputation?
Your intelligence?
Your independence?
Your religious performance?
Your ability to conceal what is really happening inside you?
You do not have to confess private details publicly to prove your sincerity.
But you do need to be honest with God.
Because the greatest danger is not always recognizing that we are weak.
Sometimes it is refusing to acknowledge that we need Him.
If this message has reached a place in your heart that you have been avoiding, take a moment and pray.

"Lord Jesus, I have trusted things that cannot save me. I have tried to control what I should have surrendered. Forgive my sins. Expose the pride, fear, and hidden compromises that keep pulling me away from You. Teach me to repent sincerely, trust Your finished work, and walk in obedience through the power of Your Spirit. I cannot rewrite my own heart. But I believe You are merciful, and I ask You to transform me. Amen."
Not as a performance.
Not to prove to strangers that you are spiritual.
But as an honest expression of where your heart is today.
And if God has already brought you through a season of repentance, restoration, or renewed faith, consider sharing a brief testimony.
Someone reading may be standing at the place where you once stood.
Wondering whether change is possible.
Wondering whether forgiveness is real.
Wondering whether Jesus still receives people who have made terrible mistakes.
Your story cannot save them.
But your testimony can point them toward the Savior who can.
And that is why sharing the gospel matters.
You may never know who needs to read it.
Perhaps a family member who has quietly drifted from faith.
A friend who looks successful but is secretly overwhelmed.
A believer who has been carrying guilt for years.
Or someone who has never truly understood why Jesus came.
Not because these words possess some special power, but because the Scriptures we have considered deserve more than a passing glance.
Return to 2 Samuel 23:20–23.
Read 1 Chronicles 11:22–25.
Then spend time with Romans 5, Ephesians 2, and 1 Corinthians 15.
Let the Word of God speak more deeply than any article ever could.
Even someone who is unsure about Christianity may be willing to begin by reading Scripture and asking sincere questions.
We want to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ, not merely to emotional moments that disappear when the screen goes dark.
Because spiritual growth requires more than inspiration.
It requires truth.
Prayer.
The Scriptures.
A life of obedience.
Fellowship with other believers.
And the daily work of the Holy Spirit shaping us into the likeness of Christ.
Our desire is to make sound biblical teaching and practical Christian resources accessible to people who are hungry for the Word.
Some readers may only be able to pray, read, share, or encourage others.
Those contributions matter.
Others may be in a position to help sustain and expand this work financially.
It can help us keep serving readers who may never be able to contribute financially.
It can help strengthen the work already being done and support its continued growth.
But I want to make something very clear.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not fear.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
But willing generosity, flowing from gratitude to God and a desire to see His Word reach more people.
Because the purpose is not to build a crowd that admires Gospel Warrior.
The purpose is to point people toward the Lord who alone can save.
And now, before we finish, return with me to that ancient battlefield.
The Egyptian warrior is standing there with his spear.
Benaiah approaches with a staff.
We know how the account ends.
The spear changes hands.
The Egyptian falls.
Benaiah's courage is remembered.
But here is the question I do not want you to forget.
When your own strength finally fails you, what will remain?
When the applause stops.
When the money cannot heal what is broken.
When your reputation cannot silence your conscience.
When your carefully constructed image can no longer hide the truth.
When you stand before God with no achievements impressive enough to erase your sins.
What will you trust?
A spear?
Yourself?
Or the crucified and risen Jesus Christ?
The Egyptian warrior's name was not preserved in the biblical account.
But the name above every name has been revealed.
Jesus.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who forgives through His blood.
The One who conquered death through His resurrection.
The One who calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And the One who can take a life that seems ruined beyond repair and make it a testimony of grace.
So do not finish this article merely impressed by Benaiah.
Let his courage remind you of the limits of human strength.
Then look to the One greater than every earthly warrior.
Turn from your sin.
Trust in Christ.
Follow Him.
And remember this:
The most dangerous thing you can carry into eternity is the belief that you never needed a Savior.
